notes.title: Devblog #2 - Guns, animations, spawning, and more!
notes.content:
[h1]Howdy![/h1]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/HmXUJGB.png[/img]
Howdy everyone, for the last several weeks I've been working on heaps of things, so I'll just break them up below into their broad categories and touch on each below:

[h1]Zombies[/h1]
The game now has zombies that can be interacted with, and they animate!


[previewyoutube=ivWoyy9e4bE;full]https://youtu.be/ivWoyy9e4bE[/previewyoutube]
[previewyoutube=a3AyFdJW1vY;full]https://youtu.be/a3AyFdJW1vY[/previewyoutube]


I've done heaps of work to setup a lot of their basic systems and get them integrated into the gameworld overall - but this isn't nearly finished yet. Lots more to do.

[h2]Zombies - Gameplay[/h2]
[previewyoutube=X4zWgZnz94c;full][/previewyoutube]
Right now the zombies respond to gameplay in a few ways:

[list]
[*] They can be shot! They recoil when hit based upon where they are shot (thanks to physical animation), and are incredibly resilient unless you shoot them in the head - in which case they drop dead almost immediately (depending on weapon calibre).
[*] They can be shoved! Zombies can be pushed away from the player, and they responding by falling in one of the 4 cardinal directions with a unique animation depending on which side they are shoved from - they then ragdoll on the floor for a bit, then they get back up.
[*] They can follow the player! Right now if they spot or hear you, they will slowly shamble in your direction.
[*] They can die! Sounds like sort of an obvious one - but there's heaps of strings attached that you don't ordinarily notice during gameplay. Dying isn't as simple as deleting the zombie, you also need to transition into a death state, then handle loot/corpse dropping, and eventually telling the zombie manager to free this zombies resources.
[/list]
[h3]Future work:[/h3]
Currently, they can't attack the player or influence them in any sort of way, but it wouldn't be much of a zombie game without that - so eventually they will not only fight back, but actively pursue you around the environment by vaulting, jumping, and falling around/out of buildings etc. I havn't started on this feature yet, but it's something i'm really excited to work on.

[h1]Weapons![/h1]
I've started properly integrating actual weapons into the game. These above are some video examples of store bought animations which I've been bringing into the weapon controllers.

[previewyoutube=BdMV5shVECU;full][/previewyoutube]
[previewyoutube=E2X-SB0GCt0;full][/previewyoutube]

The animations themselves look great - but properly setting up all the state for a multiplayer game isn't as easy as you would imagine, and is still mountains of work in its own right.

The guns can be fired, reloaded (with stages), dropped, etc - but it's mostly half done atm. I'm looking to complete your basic stock standard suite of FPS features you've come to know and love from other games.

[h3]Some screenshots:[/h3]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/nvmWz0F.png[/img]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/JMUYtHR.png[/img]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/pJdBpfi.png[/img]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/Cejqz7X.png[/img]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/zLxGrA2.png[/img]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/v5FSICv.png[/img]

[i]The above are just a collection of some of the games high powered weapons, but here's a more complete list:[/i]

[h3]Rifles:[/h3]
AK47, M16, M14, HK416, DTMDR, FAMAS, 

[h3]High power rifles:[/h3]
SVD, Kar98k, M24

[h3]Pistols:[/h3]
1911, p320, Desert eagle

[h3]Shotguns:[/h3]
Beneli M4, Ithica mag10, mossberg, spas12

[h3]SMGs[/h3]
AK74u, mp5, honeybadger, mac10, Uzi.

All the work atm is going into setting up the individual classes of firearm, tweaking their stats, their spread, ADS FOV, etc - and then later on I will give them a fresh coat of paint and sort their models out - but for now, it's all prototypey polygony type content.

[h2]Weapon handling[/h2]

I've tried a few different ways of handling weapon spread. Some methods were much more realistic then others (buckshot can brain people like a laser at 100 yards), and some were more stock standard for a vide game, and you can see the results of some of those methods below:

[img]https://i.imgur.com/3c1RdAK.png[/img]
[i]Early spread test.[/i]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/dr6Zkum.png[/img]
[i]Early spread test.[/i]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/nvB8p1P.png[/img]
[i]Early spread test.[/i]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/ju05JqL.png[/img]
[i]Early spread test.[/i]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/JP94iOs.png[/img]
[i]Early spread test.[/i]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/8oJMDNX.png[/img]
[i]Early spread test.[/i]

Final spread sight picture:
[img]https://i.imgur.com/HQ6VtdE.pnghttps://i.imgur.com/HQ6VtdE.png[/img]
Final spread sunflower pattern close up:
[img]https://i.imgur.com/OvuYfnr.png[/img]

I decided to settle on a standard spread pattern, rather then a random one. I just couldn't stomach the "realistic" gameplay of lining up a shot on a zombies head with a shotgun - and having every pellet just totally miss. It doesn't feel rewarding as a player because what we've been taught through the years is that if I aim at the enemy, and click, they take some damage - not 0 damage.

Ultimately I think what I've concluded after tweaking and playtesting, is that I want a few things:

[list]
[*] Weapon spread is a flat percentage at all times - guns just have some innate inaccuracy
[*] The weapons animation dynamically adjusts where the bullet is going out (if the player is panicked then their shaky hands will twist the sight picture sending the round off target)
[*] No spreading crosshair.
[/list]

I think if I can do these three things well, then the game will have responsive and rewarding gunplay - but there's a long way to go before than. 

[h3]Zombie spawn manager[/h3]
[previewyoutube=IdB_A40XSs4;full][/previewyoutube]
This may not look like much, but what's happening in this video is the game is accurately determining (from a list of 100 million points) which point is the closest, and which points are within a given distance (the sphere).

What is this for? The zombie spawn manager! My approach that I'm thinking for the game is to have thousands of potential spawn points littered all throughout the map, and as the player drifts close to them they will be fully instantiated into existing zombies. If the player kills that zombie - that spawn point is fully removed. 

The reason I'm going with this approach is to prevent awkward zombie respawning inside of buildings that are either 1. Closed off, or 2. Cleared/secured by the player. I can't stomach the idea that the player can build a fully enclosed sanctuary - and then have the game spawn a stray zombie in a wardrobe.

In a multiplayer game, functionality like a zombie trying to find the closest player to them in order to attack suddenly scale very poorly - and tank the games framerate. Which also means that everyone connected to the game suddenly starts lagging out and having an awful time.

Refactoring the spawn manager to only spawn zombies around connected players - with a hyper efficient lookup, is something crazy needed for making a game like this.

[h3]Summary[/h3]
If you want to follow along with the development more closely, feel free pop into the discord: 

https://discord.gg/F3pZhnzeTP

notes.title: Devblog #1 - Zombies and Inventories.
notes.content:
For the last few weeks I've been working a bunch on Inventory management, and a first pass of Zombie behaviour and visuals.

[h3]Basic Zombie Art![/h3]
I made a Zombie model for the game! It's nothing really to write home about, pretty simple, just a greyish looking bruised human with blood and tattered clothing. 

The model in Unreal: 
[img]https://i.imgur.com/yvJcSjH.png[/img]

Models in the dark:
[img]https://i.imgur.com/fOahgH2.png[/img]

It wont at all be the final art used for the zombies in the game, but I wanted something as a standin asset that could roughly approximate the costs of the final zombie models. 

Typically, I try and avoid including any art during the prototyping phase. It's too easy to become bogged down fiddling with art that you've fussed over - but this zombie only took a few hours to make, so as far as I'm concerned it's deposable! The key point is that its a clothed zombie, skeletally rendered and animated, and it has a triangle count approximately in the ballpark of the final zombies. 

This gives me a great benchmark for how many zombies can be handled on a consumer machine, and what needs to change in the art pipeline to facilitate that. At the moment they are simply skeletal meshes, but later these will probably be ported toward vertex animated textures or some sort of instancing implementation.

I have some more WIP images here (WARNING - the images contain mild nudity): 

[img]https://i.imgur.com/llQnffX.png[/img]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/h8lhIE5.png[/img]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/XOuW6ZV.png[/img]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/o3Im8Od.png[/img]

And lastly, an update of the zombies animated:

[img]https://i.imgur.com/ASjUZdU.gif[/img]

[h3]Zombie AI / sensing![/h3]
[img]https://i.imgur.com/xioqxAb.png[/img]

Zombies now have rudimentary sensing capabilities. They have a primary vision cone, and a secondary vision lost cone - basically until they are alerted, they sort of have bad vision, but once alerted they have a much wider field of view. This is to stop players sprinting right past them or hopping over them and breaking line of sight when they really shouldn't be. You can see these 2 vision cones drawn in yellow / aqua below:

[img]https://i.imgur.com/976SQgc.png[/img]

They also have a basic "memory", meaning that if they notice you through a window, and then you duck down suddenly, you won't just "vanish" in their mind - they will know where you are for a few seconds, and begin seeking you out in that area. After an extended period of time, they will eventually totally forget the players exist. I'm using the "Sense System" framework for Unreal, which is very capable and quite performant!

I've also done some work to ensure that zombies can properly navigate a dynamic environment - below you can see a visual representation of the path a zombie is attempting to take to their goal: 
[img]https://i.imgur.com/iUjKEkA.png[/img]

[h3]Zombie AI behavior![/h3]
I've also been working on the high level AI behavior of the target, and you can see an example of the state tree here:
[img]https://i.imgur.com/GqCb4Ml.png[/img]

The behaviours are pretty self explanatory - but TLDR its all the basic stuff you expect from a zombie. Meander around if they don't know you're there, but relentlessly peruse and attack you if they DO know you're there. 

Something I want to really try and expand on at a later date is zombie "signaling" - so that the player knows without double when they have been spotted by a zombie (via snarls, growls and posturing), and when they have lost them (via frustrated grunts/noises/animations)

I'm prototyping the behaviour out using Unreal 5's new "state tree" functionality, so fingers crossed it should work for everything I need it to. *fingers crossed*


[h3]Inventory management[/h3]
Heaps of work has been done so that items can now be generically moved between all inventory types. Before they were sort of jankily hardcoded just to get the feature off the ground  and working in multiplayer, and I've since gone back and generalized it.

The game has several "inventory types" - humanoid inventories, corpse inventories, map inventories, and complex procedural inventories. Why so many? Well partly because its all prototype, but also because I have to have some edge cases in a world with millions of inventory containers in multiplayer.

The player facing change is that players can now drag and drop items between their personal inventory, and either the inventories of corpses, or the equipment of those corpses (and vice versa). I think its good to prototype and iterate on the requirements of the systems (but it would have for sure been nice to get it right from the start.)

[h3]State  and Render seperation[/h3]
Previously, map meshes/chunks were coupled directly with their state - this is no longer the case. So now I have an object and a container for all the map state, and an object and container for the RENDERING of that map state. 

TLDR - I can render the map without having any state loaded for it - and once a player makes changes to a region, I can then store that state and begin replicating it in multiplayer. These changes are then spatially chunked and only replicated to players within that region. Typically with UE4 you'd have to do this with actors, but actors have such a prohibitively expensive cost when they are used at massive massive scales. So I had to come up with something a little more robust, and it seams to be working out well so far!

[h3]Summary[/h3]
Not all of the above has made it into bleeding-edge yet, but itll get there in the next few days. If you want to follow along with the development more closely, feel free pop into the discord: 

https://discord.gg/F3pZhnzeTP
